The first time I saw the ocean, I was six years old. We lived in a small inland town, miles from the nearest water, and the closest I’d ever gotten was a murky pond behind the Dollar General. So when my grandparents loaded us into their station wagon for a surprise trip to the Outer Banks, I sat pressed against the window, breath fogging the glass as the world outside turned greener, then bluer. The wind roared in my ears by the time we crossed the bridge to Kitty Hawk, and there it was—a vast, shimmering hunger, rolling and retracting like a living thing.

I remember the shock of it, not just the size, but the *sound*—the wet hiss of waves collapsing on sand, the gulls screaming, the salt spray catching in my throat. My grandfather laughed as I stumbled back when a particularly brave wave licked at my sneakers. "She’s wild," he said. "Don’t ever forget that." I didn’t. Not that day, nor the years after, when I’d return to the coast, standing at the water’s edge like some supplicant. The ocean doesn’t care if you’re the same person who left. It doesn’t judge your skin, your scars, your half-formed plans. It just keeps moving, indifferent and magnificent.

Now, when I’m restless or lost, I close my eyes and hear it—the low roar of the tide, the way it drags the world back with it. It reminds me that change isn’t something to fear. It’s the only constant worth trusting.
